'''''Silybum marianum''''' is a species of [[thistle]].  It has various [[common name]]s including '''milk thistle''',<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |access-date=2014-10-17 }}</ref> '''blessed milkthistle''',<ref>{{PLANTS|id=SIMA3|taxon=Silphium marianum|access-date=15 November 2015}}</ref> '''Marian thistle''', '''Mary thistle''', '''Saint Mary's thistle''', '''Mediterranean milk thistle''', '''variegated thistle''' and '''Scotch thistle''' (not to be confused with ''[[Onopordum acanthium]]'' or ''[[Cirsium vulgare]]''). This species is an [[annual plant|annual]] or [[biennial plant|biennial]] plant of the family [[Asteraceae]]. This fairly typical thistle has red to purple flowers and shiny pale green leaves with white veins. Once native from Southern Europe through Asia, it has spread throughout the world.

==Description==
[[Image:Illustration Silybum marianum0.jpg|thumb|Illustration]]

Milk thistle is an upright herb that can grow to be {{convert|30 to 200|cm|in|abbr=on}} tall and has an overall conical shape.<ref name="fna" /> The approximate maximum base diameter is {{convert|160|cm|in|abbr=on}}. The stem is grooved and may be covered in a light cottony fuzz.<ref name="floraofAustralia">{{cite book |url=https://profiles.ala.org.au/opus/foa/profile/Silybum%20marianum |title=Flora of Australia Volume 37: Asteraceae. |date=2015 |publisher=CSIRO Publishing |isbn=978-1-4863-0415-8 |location=Melbourne |access-date=9 August 2020}}</ref> The largest specimens have hollow stems.

The [[leaves]] are oblong to lanceolate and {{Convert|15–60|cm|abbr=on|frac=2}} long and typically [[pinnately]] lobed, with spiny edges like most thistles.<ref name="fna" /> They are hairless, shiny green, with milk-white veins.<ref name="fna">{{eFloras|1|200024549|Silybum marianum}}</ref>

The flower heads are 4 to 12 cm long and wide, of red-purple colour.  They flower from June to August in the North or December to February in the [[Southern Hemisphere]].<ref name="floraofAustralia"/> The flower head is surround by [[bract]]s which are hairless, with triangular, spine-edged appendages, tipped with a stout yellow spine.

The fruits are black [[achene]]s with a simple long white [[pappus (flower structure)|pappus]], surrounded by a yellow basal ring.<ref name="The Wild Flower Key">{{cite book |last=Rose |first=Francis |author-link=Francis Rose |title=The Wild Flower Key |year=1981 |publisher=Frederick Warne |isbn=978-0-7232-2419-8 |pages=388–9}}</ref><ref name="fna" /> A long pappus acts as a "parachute", supporting seed dispersal by wind.<ref>{{cite web |title=Milk Thistle |url=https://www.fviss.ca/invasive-plant/milk-thistle |website=www.fviss.ca |publisher=Fraser Valley Invasive Species Society |access-date=24 January 2021}}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
''Silybum marianum'' is [[Native species|native]] from around the [[Mediterranean]] and much of Europe to [[Central Asia]] and [[India]]; in Africa it reaches as far south as [[Ethiopia]].<ref name="POWO_249211-1">{{cite web |title=''Silybum marianum'' (L.) Gaertn.. |work=Plants of the World Online |publisher=Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew|url=http://www.plantsoftheworldonline.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:249211-1 |access-date=2023-04-29 }}</ref> It is possibly native near the coast of southeast England. ''S. marianum'' has been widely [[introduced species|introduced]] outside its natural range, for example into North America, [[Hawaii]], [[Australia]], [[New Zealand]], and [[Colombia]] where it is considered an [[Invasive species|invasive]] weed.<ref name="floraofAustralia"/><ref>{{cite book |last1=Bernal |last2=Gradstein |last3=Celis |title=Catálogo de plantas y líquenes de Colombia |date=2019 |publisher=Instituto de Ciencias Naturales, Universidad Nacional de Colombia |location=Bogotá |url=http://catalogoplantasdecolombia.unal.edu.co/ |archive-date=2016-04-22 |access-date=2020-08-09 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160422020259/http://catalogoplantasdecolombia.unal.edu.co/ }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Silybum marianum |url=https://plantpono.org/high-risk-plants/silybum-marianum/ |website=plantpono |access-date=9 August 2020}}</ref> It also spreads invasively in almost all of Europe as a consequence of field cultivation.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|title=Silybum marianum // Mariendistel|url=https://galasearch.de/plants/15002-silybum-marianum|website=galasearch.de}}</ref>

''Silybum marianum'' establishes itself in sunny, warm ruderal meadows in regularly disturbed places such as rubble deposits, at the foot of south-exposed walls or villages and on urban fallow land or on cattle pastures. However, it does not prefer dry, stony soils.<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite book|last=Oberdorfer|first=Erich|title=Pflanzensoziologische Exkursionsflora für Deutschland und angrenzende Gebiete|date=c. 2001|isbn=3-8001-3131-5|edition=8., stark überarb. und erg. Aufl|location=Stuttgart|page=967|oclc=50980051}}</ref>

Milk thistle has been potentially observed to modify fire regimes in its invasive range.<ref name="californiafire">{{cite journal |last1=Lambert |first1=Adam |last2=D'antonio |first2=Carla |last3=Dudley |first3=Tom |title=Invasive species and fire in California ecosystems |journal=Fremontia |date=2010 |volume=38 |issue=2 |pages=29–36 |citeseerx=10.1.1.468.2022 }}</ref><ref name="Catalina">{{cite journal |last1=Knapp |first1=John |title=CATALINA ISLAND'S INVASIVE PLANT MANAGEMENT PROGRAM, WITH AN EMPHASIS ON INVASION AND PROTECTION OF OAK ECOSYSTEMS |journal=Catalina Island Conservancy |date=2010 |volume=Proceedings of an on-island workshop, February 2–4, 2007 |pages=35–46 |url=https://www.catalinaconservancy.org/userfiles/files/wildlife/oak_symposium/08-Knapp.pdf |access-date=9 August 2020 |archive-date=7 August 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220807163245/https://www.catalinaconservancy.org/userfiles/files/wildlife/oak_symposium/08-Knapp.pdf }}</ref> Its invasion into new habitats may also be encouraged by fire.<ref name="TNCabstract">{{cite web |last1=Bean |first1=Caitiln |title=ELEMENT STEWARDSHIP ABSTRACT for Silybum marianum |url=https://www.invasive.org/gist/esadocs/documnts/silymar.pdf |publisher=The Nature Conservancy |access-date=9 August 2020}}</ref>

==Cultivation==
Milk thistle is an adaptive crop with low requirements. It is mainly cultivated as a [[medicinal plant]] but it is also sometimes used as a food source.<ref name="doi.org">Karkanis, Anestis, Dimitrios Bilalis, und Aspasia Efthimiadou. "Cultivation of Milk Thistle (Silybum Marianum L. Gaertn.), a Medicinal Weed". Industrial Crops and Products 34, Nr. 1 (1. Juli 2011): 825–30. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.indcrop.2011.03.027.</ref><ref>Qavami, N., BADI H. NAGHDI, M. R. Labbafi, und A. Mehrafarin. "A review on pharmacological, cultivation and biotechnology aspects of milk thistle (Silybum marianum (L.) Gaertn.)", 2013.</ref> It's mainly cultivated in Europe but also in Asia and North America.<ref>Zheljazkov, Valtcho D., Ivan Zhalnov, und Nedko K. Nedkov. "Herbicides for weed control in blessed thistle (Silybum marianum)". Weed technology 20, Nr. 4 (2006): 1030–1034.</ref>  Milk thistle is a [[biennial plant]], it is normally grown as an [[annual plant]], which simplifies cultivation. When the main requirements of the plant are met, then the milk thistle will blossom in the first year.<ref name="doi.org"/>

Milk thistle has low soil nutrient requirements and is drought resistant. The optimal [[pH]] ranges from 5.5 to 7.6, but a wide range is acceptable. The seeds are directly sown into the soil with a sowing depth of 1 to 1.5 cm. For [[germination]], a minimal temperature of {{Convert|2|C}} is needed. Sowing can be done in Autumn or in Spring, depending on the climate conditions. Row spacing is between 40 and 75 cm with a plant space of about 25 cm in the rows. [[Fertilization]] is not necessarily needed because of the low nutrient requirements. A standard fertilization rate of 50 kg [[nitrogen]], 30 kg [[phosphorus]] and 60 kg [[potassium]] per [[hectare]] is applied before sowing, to improve yields. Harvest normally occurs in July or August. Since the flower heads do not ripen evenly, optimal harvest time is about a [[fortnight]] after 50% of the flower heads are dry. For harvesting a common [[cereal]] [[combine harvester]] can be used. In [[Poland]], average yields are 1230 kg per ha with an average silymarin content of 26.5 kg per ha.<ref>Andrzejewska, Jadwiga, Katarzyna Sadowska, und Sebastian Mielcarek. "Effect of sowing date and rate on the yield and flavonolignan content of the fruits of milk thistle (Silybum marianum L. Gaertn.) grown on light soil in a moderate climate". Industrial Crops and Products 33, Nr. 2 (2011): 462–468.</ref>

== Chemistry ==
[[File:Silibinin skeletal.svg|thumb|right|[[Silibinin]]]]
Traditional milk thistle extract is made from the seeds (technically the whole fruit), which contain approximately 4–6% [[silymarin]].<ref name=Greenlee>{{cite journal |doi=10.1177/1534735407301727 |title=Clinical Applications of Silybum marianum in Oncology |year=2007 |last1=Greenlee |first1=H. |last2=Abascal |first2=K. |last3=Yarnell |first3=E. |last4=Ladas |first4=E. |journal=Integrative Cancer Therapies |volume=6 |issue=2 |pages=158–65 |pmid=17548794|doi-access=free }}</ref> The extract consists of about 65–80% silymarin (a [[flavonolignan]] complex) and 20–35% fatty acids, including linoleic acid.<ref name=Kroll>{{cite journal |doi=10.1177/1534735407301825 |title=Milk Thistle Nomenclature: Why It Matters in Cancer Research and Pharmacokinetic Studies |year=2007 |last1=Kroll |first1=D. J. |last2=Shaw |first2=H. S. |last3=Oberlies |first3=N. H. |journal=Integrative Cancer Therapies |volume=6 |issue=2 |pages=110–9 |pmid=17548790|doi-access=free }}</ref> In the water-soaked fruit, 41% of the mass is of the [[pericarp]] and 52% the mass is of the kernel (actual seed). Almost all of the flavolignan content is found in the pericarp.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=AbouZid |first1=SF |last2=Chen |first2=SN |last3=McAlpine |first3=JB |last4=Friesen |first4=JB |last5=Pauli |first5=GF |title=Silybum marianum pericarp yields enhanced silymarin products. |journal=Fitoterapia |date=July 2016 |volume=112 |pages=136–43 |doi=10.1016/j.fitote.2016.05.012 |pmid=27233988 |pmc=4939139 }}</ref>

Silymarin is a complex mixture of polyphenolic molecules, including seven closely related flavonolignans (silybin A, silybin B, isosilybin A, isosilybin B, silychristin, isosilychristin, silydianin) and one flavonoid ([[taxifolin]]).<ref name=Kroll/> [[Silibinin]], a semipurified fraction of silymarin, is primarily a mixture of 2 [[diastereoisomers]], silybin A and silybin B, in a roughly 1:1 ratio.<ref name=Kroll/><ref name=Hogan>{{cite journal |doi=10.1016/j.jss.2007.03.080 |title=Flavonoid, Silibinin, Inhibits Proliferation and Promotes Cell-Cycle Arrest of Human Colon Cancer |year=2007 |last1=Hogan |first1=Fawn S. |last2=Krishnegowda |first2=Naveen K. |last3=Mikhailova |first3=Margarita |last4=Kahlenberg |first4=Morton S. |journal=Journal of Surgical Research |volume=143 |pages=58–65 |pmid=17950073 |issue=1}}</ref> More complete extraction of flavonolignans from the fruit is a topic of ongoing research.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Iraqi |first1=Oumayma |last2=Jalal |first2=Mariam |last3=El Mouzazi |first3=Issam |last4=Jbene |first4=Mourad |last5=Taboz |first5=Youness |last6=Habsaoui |first6=Amar |title=Advances in Extraction Technologies of Silybum marianum L. and Its Role in Protecting Against Skin Damage |journal=Cosmetics |date=21 September 2025 |volume=12 |issue=5 |pages=211 |doi=10.3390/cosmetics12050211 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

== Toxicity ==
Milk thistle based supplements have been measured to have the highest [[mycotoxin]] concentrations of up to 37 mg/kg when compared to various plant-based dietary supplements.<ref name="pmid26168136">{{cite journal |vauthors=Veprikova Z, Zachariasova M, Dzuman Z, Zachariasova A, Fenclova M, Slavikova P, Vaclavikova M, Mastovska K, Hengst D, Hajslova J |year=2015 |title=Mycotoxins in Plant-Based Dietary Supplements: Hidden Health Risk for Consumers |journal=Journal of Agricultural and Food Chemistry |volume=63 |issue=29 |pages=6633–43 |doi=10.1021/acs.jafc.5b02105 |pmid=26168136 |bibcode=2015JAFC...63.6633V |quote=The highest mycotoxin concentrations were found in milk thistle-based supplements (up to 37 mg/kg in the sum).}}</ref>

Use of milk thistle may cause stomach upset and produce [[Allergy|allergic reactions]] in some people.<ref name="nccih" /> There is a documented case of a 29-year-old employee at an organic food production facility who was found to have an isolated allergy to milk thistle. The allergy developed through inhalation, and clinical symptoms (runny nose, sneezing, watery and burning eyes, and wheezing) did not appear until a few years after the period of direct work involving the packaging of ground milk thistle fruit. The patient reported that he had never previously consumed milk thistle in the form of infusions or dietary supplements. The patient described was also found to have an allergy to ''Eragrostis tef'', wasp venom, and hypersensitivity to certain raw fruits and vegetables. It is anticipated that the growing popularity of milk thistle-based products in the food and pharmaceutical industries may lead to more frequent recognition of hypersensitivity to this plant.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Wojas |first1=O. |last2=Krzych-Fałta |first2=E. |last3=Samel-Kowalik |first3=P. |last4=Żalikowska-Gardocka |first4=M. |last5=Majsiak |first5=E. |last6=Mari |first6=A. |last7=Samoliński |first7=B. |date=2020-04-15 |title=A case of allergy to Silybum marianum (milk thistle) and Eragrostis tef (teff) |journal=Allergy, Asthma & Clinical Immunology |language=en |volume=16 |issue=1 |pages=23 |doi=10.1186/s13223-020-00421-5 |doi-access=free |issn=1710-1492 |pmc=7161110 |pmid=32322285}}</ref> Eyelid edema, ocular pruritus, dry eye, diplopia, and blurred vision are among the reported complications based on registered side effects in the [[WHO]] global database of adverse drug reactions.<ref>{{cite journal |date=2025 |title=Potential therapeutic effects of milk thistle (Silybum marianum) in eye diseases, a scoping review |journal=Discover Applied Sciences |volume=7 |issue=17 |doi=10.1007/s42452-024-06401-3 |doi-access=free |last1=Tahmasbi |first1=Zahra |last2=Boroughani |first2=Mohadese |last3=Heidari |first3=Mohamad Mahdi |last4=Namvar |first4=Ehsan |last5=Hashempur |first5=Mohammad Hashem |last6=Faraji |first6=Seyed Nooreddin |last7=Nazarpour-Servak |first7=Mostafa |last8=Heydari |first8=Mojtaba |article-number=17 }}</ref>

===Leaf toxicity===
{{see also|Nitrate#Toxicity and safety}}
Because of [[nitrate]]<ref name="floraofAustralia" /> content, the leaf has been found to be toxic to cattle and sheep.<ref name="floraofAustralia" /> When potassium nitrate is eaten by [[ruminant]]s, the bacteria in the animal's stomach breaks the chemical down, producing nitrite ions. Nitrite ions then combine with [[hemoglobin]] to produce [[methemoglobin]], blocking the transport of oxygen. The result is a form of [[oxygen deprivation]].<ref>http://ucanr.edu/sites/UCCE_LR/files/180507.pdf  Tucker JM, et al. Nitrate Poisoning in Livestock (1961)</ref>

== Uses ==
Although potentially allergenic, the leaves and stems can be gathered ahead of bloom, the spines removed, and boiled with salt.<ref name="tfb">{{Cite book |last=Francis-Baker |first=Tiffany |title=Concise Foraging Guide |date=2021 |publisher=[[Bloomsbury Publishing|Bloomsbury]] |isbn=978-1-4729-8474-6 |series=[[The Wildlife Trusts]] |location=London |page=81}}</ref> The roots are edible raw or roasted and the flower head can be cooked like globe [[artichoke]].<ref name="tfb" />

Silymarin is extracted from the milk thistle seeds (technically the fruits) and available as a standardized extract.<ref>{{Citation|last=Bhattacharya|first=Sanjib|chapter=Chapter 90 - Milk Thistle (Silybum marianum L. Gaert.) Seeds in Health|date=2011-01-01|chapter-url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/B9780123756886100908|title=Nuts and Seeds in Health and Disease Prevention|pages=759–766|editor-last=Preedy|editor-first=Victor R.|place=San Diego|publisher=Academic Press|language=en|isbn=978-0-12-375688-6|access-date=2021-12-02|editor2-last=Watson|editor2-first=Ronald Ross|editor3-last=Patel|editor3-first=Vinood B.}}</ref> In 2018, the [[European Medicines Agency]] published an assessment report on the oral use of milk thistle fruit and its extracts in EU states. It finds that there is a "well-established use" of hepatoprotection approved by 11 countries and a "traditional use" of [[Indigestion|dyspeptic]] complaints in 4 countries. EMA has also published a [[monograph]] on this herbal substance.<ref>{{cite web |title=Assessment report on Silybum marianum (L.) Gaertn., fructus EMA/HMPC/294188/2013|website=European Medicines Agency (EMA) |url=https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/medicines/herbal/silybi-mariani-fructus |language=en |date=31 December 2009}}</ref>

Although milk thistle "seed" (fruit) has been used in [[traditional medicine]] for centuries, there is no [[Evidence-based medicine|clinical evidence]] that it has any medicinal effect as of the year 2020.<ref name="nccih">{{cite web|date=1 August 2020|title=Milk thistle|url=https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/milk-thistle|access-date=20 October 2020|publisher=National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health, US National Institutes of Health}}</ref><ref name="rainone">{{cite journal|last1=Rainone|first1=Francine|year=2005|title=Milk Thistle|url=http://www.aafp.org/link_out?pmid=16225032|journal=American Family Physician|volume=72|issue=7|pages=1285–8|pmid=16225032}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|vauthors=Rambaldi A, Jacobs BP, Gluud C|year=2007|title=Milk thistle for alcoholic and/or hepatitis B or C virus liver diseases|journal=The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews|volume=2009 |issue=4|article-number=CD003620|doi=10.1002/14651858.CD003620.pub3|pmid=17943794|s2cid=41057368 |pmc=8724782}}</ref> In 2019, [[Cancer Research UK]] stated: "We need a lot more research with reliable clinical trials before we can be sure that milk thistle will play any part in treating or preventing cancers."<ref>{{cite web|date=9 May 2019|title=Milk thistle and liver cancer|url=http://www.cancerresearchuk.org/about-cancer/cancers-in-general/cancer-questions/milk-thistle-and-liver-cancer|access-date=9 August 2020|publisher=Cancer Research UK}}</ref>

There have been concerns about product safety. For example, the amount of silymarin noted on the product label may differ significantly from the actual amount contained in the product. There have also been findings of contamination with [[pesticides]], [[microorganisms]] and [[mycotoxins]].<ref name="nccih"/>
